title: AWS global infrastructure: Regions, Availability Zones and edge locations
learningObjective: Describe Regions, Availability Zones and edge locations, how they relate, how to achieve high availability with multiple AZs, and when to use multiple Regions.
foundation: A Region is a geographic area (for example eu-west-1, Ireland) with several Availability Zones.
An Availability Zone (AZ) is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking and connectivity, isolated from other AZs but connected by fast, low-latency links.
Edge locations are sites near users that CloudFront, Route 53 and Global Accelerator use to deliver content and DNS quickly.
engineer: Regions are fully isolated from each other; most services are Regional, some are global (IAM, Route 53, CloudFront). Choose a Region by compliance/data sovereignty, proximity to users, service availability and price.

AZs: each Region has at least three AZs; AZs are physically separated so they do not share single points of failure. Deploy across at least two AZs with Elastic Load Balancing and Auto Scaling; managed services offer Multi-AZ options (RDS Multi-AZ, S3 stores data across AZs by default for most classes).
Multiple Regions: disaster recovery and business continuity, low latency for global users, data sovereignty requirements, and resilience to Regional events.

Edge: CloudFront caches content; Route 53 answers DNS at the edge; Global Accelerator routes users over the AWS network. Local Zones place compute closer to population centers; Wavelength Zones sit in telecom 5G networks.

example.title: Resilient e-commerce
body: The shop runs in three AZs in Frankfurt behind an Application Load Balancer, with RDS Multi-AZ. A pilot-light copy in another Region covers Regional disasters, and CloudFront serves images worldwide.

prerequisites: An AWS account (use an IAM Identity Center user, not root)
permissions: Read-only access to explore; least-privilege permissions to change resources
limits: Conceptual objective: explore in the console; no configuration limits are tested
portal: EC2 > Launch instance > Subnet: choose AZs.

troubleshooting.fix: Spread across AZs with ELB and Auto Scaling.

troubleshooting.symptom: Slow for users on another continent.

comparisons.difference: Equivalent; Azure also defines region pairs.

misconceptions.myth: An AZ is a single data center.
misconceptions.reality: An AZ is one or more data centers.
They host CloudFront/Route 53 and similar edge services.

architectureDecisions: Multi-AZ for high availability; multi-Region for DR, latency or sovereignty.

walkthrough.subtitle: Place one app on the AWS map: pick a Region, spread across AZs, add Regions and edge locations.
learn: Regions, Availability Zones and edge locations
AZs share no single points of failure

steps.label: Where?
steps.title: Where should your app live?
body: Your users are in Europe. If one data center fails the app must keep running, and next year you expand to Japan.
You need to understand AWS's map: Regions, AZs and edge locations.

steps.label: Region
steps.title: A Region is a geographic area
body: A Region, for example Europe (Ireland), is a separate geographic area. You choose the Region for each resource, based on where users are, data rules, service availability and price.
Data stays in the Region you pick unless you move it.

steps.label: AZs
steps.title: Each Region has several Availability Zones
body: An Availability Zone is one or more data centers with their own power, cooling and networking. A Region has several AZs (normally at least three), kilometres apart but linked by fast, low-latency connections.
Because AZs don't share single points of failure, a fire or power cut in one doesn't take down the others.

steps.label: Multi-AZ
steps.title: Run in multiple AZs for high availability
body: Put servers in at least two AZs behind a load balancer, and use a Multi-AZ database. If AZ a fails, traffic flows to b and c.
This is AWS's basic recipe for high availability.

callout.text: High availability within a Region = multiple AZs. One AZ alone is a single point of failure.

steps.label: Multi-Region
steps.title: Add Regions when you need them
body: Use more than one Region for disaster recovery and business continuity if a whole Region fails, for low latency for users on other continents, or for data sovereignty laws that require data to stay in a country.
Multi-Region costs more and is harder, so do it for a reason.

steps.label: Edge
steps.title: Edge locations bring content closer
body: Edge locations are many smaller sites in cities worldwide. CloudFront caches content there, Route 53 answers DNS there, and Global Accelerator routes traffic onto the AWS network there.
Users get faster responses because the first hop is close.

callout.text: Edge locations don't run your EC2 servers. They cache and route; your app runs in a Region.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: Region → AZs → edge
body: Many edge locations at the edge; inside each Region, isolated AZs.
recap: Region = geographic area; AZ = isolated data center(s) in a Region
AZs share no single points of failure
Multi-Region for DR, latency and data sovereignty
Edge locations: CloudFront, Route 53, Global Accelerator
